about: Real pages, read by the app and checked by a person.  The synthetic corpus in
tests/fixtures says what the geometry can do on engraving it has never seen fail;
this says what it does on the photocopied jazz voicings the app is actually for.
Every note list here is ground truth a person supplied, unless the entry's note
says it was inferred.  null means nobody has checked that hand of that step.
known_wrong lists the entries the reader currently gets wrong, so they are tracked
rather than ignored: tests/test_pages.py fails when one of them starts passing,
which is the signal to move it out of known_wrong.
clefs, where given, is each system's clefs top to bottom, checked as one entry named clefs.
Pitch names are ASCII, as in the fixture manifest: F#4, Bb2.

pages.note: Giant Steps, first line, a textbook page photographed.  Every step annotated by the owner.  The reader currently finds 8 events for 6 chords: a lone F3 appears as a sixth event and a seventh is the last chord read twice, so steps after 5 do not line up by index.

The same line of Giant Steps at lower resolution, as the app's own straightened output.  Same ground truth.  Step 3's F sharp is a sharp broken into pieces by staff line removal and not yet read; step 5's E flat in the left hand is missed.  The seventh event used to be a false positive: the final barline, read as a ladder of noteheads.

Search for Peace.  The owner reported step 1 missing a right-hand note and its left-hand note, its E flat read as E, and step 5's F read as F sharp.  Step 1's G3 and A2 are inferred: they complete the A half-diminished the page labels the chord as, and are what the reader now finds.  Confirm them.  Step 5's left hand has two sharps fused with their noteheads into one shape that nothing reads yet, so it is unchecked.
Sophisticated Lady.  Steps 1 and 2 annotated by the owner.  The G in step 2 is G3, the octave the reader finds; the owner gave the letter only.

A short grand staff in B flat whose staff lines slope about two pixels across the page.  The bass staff's span was measured from one pixel row of its top line and came out 232px short, which put its clef outside detect_clef's window and started the notehead search after the first chord: the whole left hand of it went missing, and the staff's own key signature with it.  Steps 2 and 3 are the two ends of a tie and carry the same pitches.  Read off the image rather than supplied by the owner, and checked against the ledger lines and the augmentation dots, which sit at their own notehead's height.

The same opening as jamesmay.png and more of the piece.  Here the coarse skew estimate, made on a 900px wide copy where a fifth of a degree hardly moves the score, picked the wrong side of a flat maximum and rotated a level page to 0.2 degrees off: nine pixels of drift end to end, both staves measuring short, neither clef read, no key signature found on either, and the first chord never looked for.  Only steps 1 to 3 are annotated, being the same music as jamesmay.png; the triplets and the five-note chord later on have not been checked by anyone.

One flat, and the flat of the signature is drawn with a long ascender: its bowl measured 0.28 spaces high, over half a step, so the run read as a C rather than a B and the page came out in C major with every B in it natural.  It also had a beam read as a note over the first chord, which moved that chord's label off the note it belonged to, and its final barline read as a ladder of three notes in each hand.  The owner reported all of those.  Steps 12 and 13 are theirs too: the C-7 is G, E flat, B flat and the F7 keeps the E flat, and both E flats are still read as E because the flat that says so is fused with the noteheads it sits against.  Two spurious notes remain, on step 5 and step 7, both on a slanted beam whose ink is too short on any one row to tell from a notehead.  Everything else here is unchecked.

Four grand staffs in G, photocopied.  The page that took clef reading out.  The treble clef, the sharp and the 4/4 cut the first hundred pixels of every treble staff line into runs too short to count as line, so each treble staff measured as starting after them, the clef sat outside the glyph search, and the 4 of the time signature was read as a bass clef; the grand staff's two bass clefs were then settled by confidence, and which hand was swapped differed between builds.  The third system's two staves both measured short, so the window for the barline joining them missed it and they were read as two lone staves.  Now paired by a window anchored at the page's margin, lined up on the bass staff's edge, and named by position.  The third system's edges are both short, so its key signature is still not seen: that is the key entry in known_wrong.  The steps annotated are read off the image rather than supplied by the owner.  Steps 9, 16, 17, 24, 28 and 50 each have a right-hand note two ledger lines or more below the treble, past the midpoint of a gap 3.6 spaces wide, where the bass either claimed it as a D4 with the whole note's own rim as the ledger line or threw it away.  Both staves now search the whole gap and a note goes to the staff whose ledger lines are really there.  Step 8's B flat sat across the old edge of the treble's band, cut in half for the classifier, and is read now that the search reaches across the gap.  Two right hands are left out because a tie carries an accidental across the barline into them (steps 9 and 17), which the reader does not follow.  The flat before the bass's B2 in step 16 is printed touching the notehead and is not read (16.left); step 28's right hand reads two peaks on one half note and folds in the quarter note beside it (28.right).
